notes: Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Orange zoned cap, orange latex scrobicules on the stem, orange gills. Saffron milkcap group; L. deterrimus is the spruce one and is not in the label space, so a mycologist might split this.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED: Craterellus tubaeformis, yellowfoot. NOT one of the 244, so the app should decline rather than name anything.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Grey-brown hollow funnel, wavy margin. Horn of plenty.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. In situ, red cap with white warts. The easiest case in the set.

CONFIRMED by Martin, 2026-10-29: Mycena rosea. I read it as rosea-or-pura and could not separate them from the photograph; both are in the label space and both TOXIC, so this stays the most interesting row in the set.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Netted white stem, brown cap. Penny bun.
Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Small bolete, dark red-brown cap, yellow stem in moss. Could be Imleria badia or a Neoboletus; the cap colour and size lean Xerocomellus.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Blue-green cups on a fallen stick. Green elfcup.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Two large pale caps, margin inrolled, a buff-grey flush at the centre, on moss under spruce. Clouded funnel is the obvious call and the gills are not visible, which is exactly where that call would have been made or lost. Leucopaxillus giganteus and a white Lactarius are not excluded and neither is in the label space.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Wholly blackened, thick distant gills, stout pale stem with a cracked surface. Blackening brittlegill. Note this is the species docs/SPECIES.md already asks the reviewer about: both nomenclators make R. nigricans a synonym of R. adusta, so the images behind this label are adusta's.
Claude's reading. Red cap with white warts, white free gills, pendulous ring, ringed bulbous base. Every diagnostic character in one frame -- the control for the set.

Claude CANNOT determine this one. Two fruiting bodies on mud among oak litter: the left shows a plain brown cap and a dirty pale stem, the right crowded cream gills flecked brown. Tricholoma is the genus that keeps suggesting itself and I am not confident past that. The most valuable row in the batch if Martin knows it.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Pale tan caps, free PINK gills, slender stems rising from a white sheathing base in grass. Stubble rosegill. Pink gills plus a volva is the combination that matters: the one Amanita-shaped silhouette that is not an Amanita.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Dense cream-brown ruffled mass at the foot of a conifer. Wood cauliflower. No cap, no gills, no spore print, so the interrogation engine has almost nothing to ask -- which is why it is worth having.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE, and deliberately the same guess as 09 from a different angle and a different wood. Smooth cream cap, stout fibrous white stem, held in the hand. They may well be two species and I cannot tell; if the model separates them it is telling us something.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED: Lycoperdon pyriforme, stump puffball. Small pale puffballs in a row ON A MOSSY LOG, and growing on wood is the character that names it -- the other puffballs here are on soil. NOT one of the 245, so the app should decline. It is also one of the gaps: very common, and its genus is already in the label space.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED: Coprinopsis picacea, magpie inkcap. Conical, black, with large white felty patches. NOT one of the 245, and distinctive enough that a user would expect an answer -- which makes it a good test of whether a refusal reads as a failure.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Tawny-orange cap with a striate margin, pale stem, large white saccate volva, and no ring that I can see. Tawny grisette. A. crocea is not in the label space and A. vaginata is -- the grisette the twelve were added for -- so this row sits directly on the 'a bag at the base means danger' argument.
Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Pear-shaped puffballs in moss, covered in conical warts. Common puffball. Pairs with 16 and 27: three puffballs, only two of which the app has a name for.

Claude CANNOT determine this one, and it is the one I least want to guess at. Greasy brown cap, stout white stem with pale fibrous veil remnants, gills that look rusty brown. Cortinarius is what that adds up to; the two deadly webcaps are in the label space, so a wrong label here would poison exactly the comparison this set exists to make.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Brown cap, yellow pores bruising blue-green where damaged, plain brown stem with no network. Bay bolete. Row 07 is the other possibility and both are in the label space.
Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE: Phaeolus schweinitzii, dyer's mazegill. Yellow growing margin, rust-brown velvety centre, guttation droplets, at a conifer base. NOT one of the 245.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE, and the most consequential guess in the batch. Grey-brown cap with pure white patches, white stem with a ring and a distinctly collared bulb. Panther cap is SERIOUS; A. excelsa (no recorded toxicity) and A. rubescens (TOXIC) are both in the label space and both are what it is if I am wrong. Nobody should quote a result from this row until Martin has looked at it.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Shaggy-scaled cap, tall snakeskin stem, movable ring, in rough grass. Parasol. Chlorophyllum rhacodes (TOXIC) and the deadly Lepiota are the neighbourhood that makes it worth grading.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. A single sulphur-yellow mushroom on rotten wood, olive-tinted gills, curved stem. Sulphur tuft. Same species as 26 as a lone specimen: growing in a dense tuft is half of what names it in the field, and the model only sees pixels.

Claude's reading, UNCONFIRMED. Dense tuft on a stump, tawny-centred yellow caps, crowded olive gills. Sulphur tuft -- and the funeral bell and honey fungus are precisely the neighbourhood this photograph sits in.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Large elongated white warty puffball in grass; pestle puffball. This row is A SCREENSHOT, phone status bar and all, rather than a photograph. People will hand the app pictures of pictures and nothing else here tests that.

Claude's reading, LOW CONFIDENCE. Brown cap, strongly red stem, yellow flesh showing where it is cut, in rough grass. Scarletina bolete -- one of the six species with zero iNaturalist images, so whatever the model does here it does on a thin and unusually sourced training set.
